{{Orphan|date=March 2021}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''K transform''' (also called the '''Single-Pixel X-ray Transform''') is an [[integral transform]] introduced by [[R. Scott Kemp]] and [[Ruaridh Macdonald]] in 2016.<ref name="original paper">{{cite journal|last1=Kemp|first1=R. Scott|last2=Danagoulian|first2=Areg|last3=Macdonald|first3=Ruaridh R.|last4=Vavrek|first4=Jayson|display-authors=1|title=Physical cryptographic verification of nuclear warheads|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=August 2, 2016|volume=113|issue=31|pages=8618–8623|doi=10.1073/pnas.1603916113|pmid=27432959|pmc=4978267|bibcode=2016PNAS..113.8618K|doi-access=free}}</ref> The transform allows the structure of a N-dimensional inhomogeneous object to be reconstructed from scalar point measurements taken in the volume external to the object.

[[Gunther Uhlmann]] proved<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kemp|first1=R. Scott|last2=Danagoulian|first2=Areg|last3=Macdonald|first3=Ruaridh R.|last4=Vavrek|first4=Jayson|display-authors=1|title=Supporting information: physical cryptographic verification of nuclear warheads|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=August 2, 2016|volume=113|issue=31|pages=SI-5|doi=10.1073/pnas.1603916113|pmid=27432959|pmc=4978267|url=https://www.pnas.org/content/pnas/suppl/2016/07/13/1603916113.DCSupplemental/pnas.1603916113.sapp.pdf|access-date=22 Feb 2021|doi-access=free}}</ref> that the K&nbsp;transform exhibits global uniqueness on <math>\mathbb R^n</math>, meaning that different objects will always have a different K&nbsp;transform.  This uniqueness arises from the use of a monotone, nonlinear transform of the [[X-ray transform]]. By selecting the [[exponential function]] for the monotone nonlinear function, the behavior of the K transform coincides with attenuation of particles in matter as described by the [[Beer–Lambert law]], and the K&nbsp;transform can therefore be used to perform [[tomography]] of objects using a low-resolution single-pixel detector. 

An inversion formula based on a linearization was offered by Lai et al., who also showed that the inversion is stable under certain assumptions.<ref name="Lai">

==Definition==
Let an object <math>f</math> be a function of compact support that maps into the positive real numbers
<math display="block">f:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+}_0 .</math>
The K-transform of the object <math>f</math> is defined as
<math display="block">\mathcal{K}:L^1(\Omega,\mathbb{P}^{+}_0)\rightarrow[0,1],</math>
<math display="block">\mathcal{K}f(r)\equiv\int_{L_D(r)}e^{\mathcal{P}f(l)}\,dl,</math>
where <math>L_D(r)\equiv L(r)\cap L(D)</math> is the set of all lines originating at a point <math>r</math> and terminating on the single-pixel detector <math>D</math>, and <math>\mathcal{P}</math> is the [[X-ray transform]].

== Proof of global uniqueness ==
Let <math>\mathcal{P}f</math> be the [[X-ray transform]] transform on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> and let <math>\mathcal{K}</math> be the non-linear operator defined above. Let <math>L^1</math> be the space of all Lebesgue integrable functions on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> , and <math>L^\infty</math> be the [[Essential infimum and essential supremum|essentially bounded]] measurable functions of the dual space. The following result says that <math>-\mathcal{K}</math> is a monotone operator.

For <math>f,g\in L^1</math> such that <math>\mathcal{K}f,\mathcal{K}g\in L^\infty</math> then
<math display="block">\langle\mathcal{K}f-\mathcal{K}g,f-g\rangle\leq 0</math>
and the inequality is strict when <math>f\neq g</math>.

<em>Proof.</em> Note that <math>\mathcal{P}f(r,\theta)</math> is constant on lines in direction <math>\theta</math>, so <math>\mathcal{P}f(r,\theta)=\mathcal{P}f(E_\theta r,\theta)</math>, where <math>E_\theta</math> denotes orthogonal projection on <math>\theta^\bot</math>.  Therefore:

<math display="block">
\langle\mathcal{K}f-\mathcal{K}g,f-g\rangle =\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}} \left(e^{-\mathcal{P}f(r,\theta)}-e^{-\mathcal{P}g(r,\theta)}\right)(f-g)(r)\,d\theta\, dr</math>

<math display="block">=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \left(e^{-\mathcal{P}f(r,\theta)}-e^{-\mathcal{P}g(r,\theta)}\right)(f-g)(r)\,dr\,d\theta</math>

<math display="block">=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\theta^\bot} \left(e^{-\mathcal{P}f(E_\theta r,\theta)}-e^{-\mathcal{P}g(E_\theta r,\theta)}\right)\int_\mathbb{R}(f-g)(E_\theta r+s\theta)\,ds\,dr_{\!H}\,d\theta</math>

<math display="block">=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\theta^\bot} \left(e^{-\mathcal{P}f(E_\theta r,\theta)}-e^{-\mathcal{P}g(E_\theta r,\theta)}\right)\left(\mathcal{P}f(E_\theta r,\theta)-\mathcal{P}g(E_\theta r,\theta)\right)dr_{\!H}\,d\theta
</math>

where <math>dr_{\!H}</math> is the [[Lebesgue measure]] on the [[hyperplane]] <math>\theta^\bot</math>. The integrand has the form <math>(e^{-s}-e^{-t})(s-t)</math>, which is negative except when <math>s=t</math> and so <math>\langle\mathcal{K}f-\mathcal{K}g,f-g\rangle<0</math> unless <math>\mathcal{P}f=\mathcal{P}g</math> almost everywhere. Then uniqueness for the X-Ray transform implies that <math>g=f</math> [[almost everywhere]]. <math>\blacksquare</math>

Lai et al. generalized this proof to [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian manifolds]].<ref name="Lai" /> 

== Applications ==
The K transform was originally developed as a means of performing a physical [[one-time pad]] encryption of a physical object.<ref name="original paper" /> The nonlinearity of the transform ensures the there is no one-to-one correspondence between the density <math>f</math> and the true mass <math>\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_\mathbb{R}f(x+s\theta)\,ds\,d\theta</math>, and therefore <math>f</math> cannot be estimated from a single projection.
